title: "Data Science"
subtitle: "A 16-session course, from a raw CSV to a deployed model"
---

::: {.callout-note}
**This is a book you read alone.** Every idea is explained from the beginning, every term
is defined the first time it appears, and **every piece of code on these pages actually
ran** when the book was built. The numbers you see are the numbers the code produced.

**Every demonstration loads a real file.** Nothing is typed into the program as a Python
list, because that is not how data arrives. The files live in
[`datasets/`](https://github.com/) and are read the way a real project reads them:

```python
df = pd.read_csv("datasets/messy_customers.csv")
```
:::

## Who this is for

Anyone who wants to work with data and has **no prior background** in statistics, machine
learning, or Python. Session 1 assumes you can use a computer. Nothing else.

## How the course is built

Sixteen sessions in five parts. Each part exists because the one before it is not enough
on its own.

| Part | Sessions | The question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Getting hold of data** | 1–2 | What is this field, and how do I load a dataset? |
| **B — Making data fit to use** | 3–6 | It is messy, scattered and too wide. Now what? |
| **C — Understanding data** | 7–8 | What is actually in here? |
| **D — Learning from data** | 9–12 | What can be predicted, is it real, and how do others use it? |
| **E — Data at scale** | 13–16 | What changes when it no longer fits on one machine? |

## How each session is written

Every session follows the same shape, so once you have read two you can predict the third.

| Element | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Demo** | runnable code that demonstrates one idea. Most sessions have eight to fifteen. |
| 🧠 **Analogy** | an everyday comparison — used only where a concept genuinely needs one |
| ⚠️ **Trap** | a mistake that produces a wrong answer **without raising an error** |
| 🔓 **Key idea** | something you must carry into later sessions |
| ❓ **Check yourself** | short questions with worked answers, folded away |
| ✏️ **Tasks** | things to do, with solutions folded away |
| ✅ **Before you move on** | the checklist for that session |

::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 What makes this course different"}
**Nothing here is asserted without being measured.** Where a demonstration contradicted
the lesson it was written for, the lesson was changed and the number kept. You will
find, among other things:

- 80% accuracy manufactured from **coin flips**, by one careless line
- a model saved without its scaler, valuing a flat at **₹1.69 billion** instead of ₹5 million
- a polynomial that fits its training data best and scores **−187** on new data
- a "best" model chosen by peeking, reported at +0.08 and worth **−0.20** in truth
- K-Means confidently finding three clusters in **pure random noise**

Those are the passages that teach the most, because they are what you will actually meet.
:::

## The data

Eight of the datasets are **real published files** — a car marketplace, a loan book, mall
customers, heart-failure patients. The rest are **generated by a seeded script** in the
`datasets/` folder, and only where a chapter needs a property no real file has: a known
cluster structure, a planted association rule, a deliberate leak.

| | |
|---|---|
| Rebuild every generated file | `python datasets/make_all.py` |
| Re-download the real ones | `python datasets/download_real.py` |
| What each file is for | [`datasets/README.md`](datasets/README.md) |

The formats vary on purpose — CSV, JSON, plain text, Excel, SQL, and one table split
across several files — because real data does not arrive in one shape.

## Setting up

All code runs in one conda environment. Create it once:

```bash
conda create -n ds python=3.11 -y
conda activate ds
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Then build the book with `quarto render`, or open any session and run the cells in
Jupyter. **Every session is self-contained** — variables do not carry from one to the
next, so you can start anywhere, though the order is designed to be read straight
through.

## A note on the order

Sessions 3–6 prepare data; Sessions 7–8 describe it. If you have met this material
before you may expect statistics to come first — it is the more common arrangement.

Session 3 borrows the two ideas it needs (quartiles and standard deviation) in a marked
box, so nothing is used before it is explained, and Session 7 then covers them properly.
**If you prefer, read Sessions 7 and 8 before Session 3.** Nothing in them depends on
Sessions 3–6.
